They all brought out their fields and houses to set Cheng up. His brothers were furious at this show of generosity and went to his door to shame and insult him. Cheng had lived among bandits for a long time and was accustomed to violence. He heard of this and was greatly enraged, saying, "I have returned, yet no one is willing to provide me with a single room. Fortunately, my third younger brother remembered our sibling bond, and yet you condemn him for it. Do you wish to drive me away?" He threw a stone at Xiao, who fell. Ren and Yi each brought out a staff and went to seize Zhong and Xin, beating them both repeatedly. Cheng did not wait for them to sue him; he sued them first before the magistrate. The magistrate sent for Youyu, who had no choice but to appear. He bowed his head and said nothing, only shedding tears. When pressed for an answer, he requested only that the magistrate investigate the matter. The magistrate ruled that Xiao and the others should each contribute a portion of their land to restore Cheng, ensuring all seven shares were equal. From this point on, Ren, Yi, and Cheng grew even more affectionate and respectful toward one another. During a conversation, they suddenly touched upon the burial of their mother, and all began to weep. Cheng said in anger, "To be so unfilial is to behave like beasts." He then intended to open the grave and rebury her. Ren and Yi ran to inform Youyu, who hurried back to remonstrate and stop him. Cheng would not listen and set a date.

<summary>This passage describes a family conflict where the protagonist Cheng, emboldened by his time among bandits, uses violence and legal action to force his brothers to redistribute family property, later culminating in an attempt to rebury their mother.</summary>
<keywords>family conflict, inheritance, filial piety, magistrate, reburial, Cheng, Xiao, Ren, Yi, Youyu</keywords>
